newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court says Commission acted correctly to refuse CFC licence.
newsitem.headline: Court says Commission acted correctly to refuse CFC licence.

text.p: The European Court of First Instance dismissed on Wednesday claims that the European Commission acted unlawfully when it refused to grant import licences for chlorofluorocarbons 11 (CFC 11).

Under Community regulations, the Commission sets annual limits for ozone-depleting substances allowed to enter the EU. Once quotas are allocated, an undertaking must apply to the Commission for an import licence.

Efisol, a French company, was listed among importers by the Commission as eligible to receive CFC 11 quotas. Efisol then applied for import licences, but was denied when the French government disputed the application, stating that Efisol's planned use for the CFCs was not feedstock for the manufacture of other chemicals, but to make other products.
After applying for the licence, but before the Commission denied the application, Efisol purchased orders from its Russian supplier.

When the Commission refused to grant the licence, Efisol brought an action for damages sustained as a result of its orders, especially to cover transportation costs. The Commission rejected any claim from Efisol, stressing that any serious misconduct had to be attributed to the applicant, which had attempted to mislead the Commission as to the exact use to which the substances were to be put, the court's judgment said.
Efisol claimed the Commission breached the principle of legitimate expectations, arguing that once the quota had been allocated, the Commission was required to issue a licence.

The Commission told the court it would never have allocated the quota if it had understood Efisol wanted to import CFC 11 to produce polyurethane foam, and not as feedstock to manufacture other chemicals.

In light of Community regulations, the court said "the applicant could not, in good faith, have expected that import licences would be issued to it. No expectation could be derived from the allocation to it of an import quota, since that is merely the first stage in securing an effective right to import a substance."
(Court translation into English. Original language of the case: French)
"Regulation (EEC) No 594/91 on substances that deplete the ozone layer - Import licences - Refusal to grant - Application for compensation - Protection of legitimate expectations"
Commission of the European Commission, defendant

application under article 178 and the second paragraph of article 215 of the EC Treaty seeking compensation for the damage occasioned by the refusal to grant licences to import chlorofluorcarbon 11 into the Community
THE COURT OF FIRST INSTANCE hereby
2. Orders the Commission to pay the whole of the costs.
